html:
The Puruborá are a small Tupian people of the state of Rondônia in western Brazil, in the valley of the Manoel Correia River, a tributary of the Guaporé. Their language forms its own branch of the Tupian family, related distantly to that of the Tupi.

In the early 1900s rubber tappers, and then the government's Indian Protection Service, moved many Puruborá off their land and into rubber work during the rubber boom, and their families were scattered. For decades officials treated them as extinct. In the 2000s descendants came together again, claimed their identity and land, and began to record the last speakers of their language. About 200 people count themselves Puruborá today. See Brazil.
